items.title: [FDD Diary #4] The Real Problem
content:
Not the AI's fault.
"Make a date format function." It did. Good work.
"Parse the config." It did. Clean job.
AI did exactly what I asked. Every single time.

Not the prompt's fault either.
"In this format." "This data." "Process it like this."
Specific enough.

So why did ten thousand lines of tangled spaghetti come out?
Why did the same function get built five times?
Why was there a security hole?

I didn't know what I was building.

"Connect three computers." That's a wish, not a design.

Monday: "Let's do file sync first."
Wednesday: "Wait, shouldn't screen sharing come first?"
Friday: "Remote commands are the most urgent."

Direction changed every time.
AI built in that direction every time.
Every time convincing. Every time different. Every time slightly wrong.

AI doesn't say "Hey, last week we were doing file sync. Why suddenly screen sharing?"
It just follows orders. Silently.

I can't read code.
Can't tell what was built before.
So every time, AI built from scratch.
The same thing. A different way. Five times.

Making files? Free. Claude does it.
Writing functions? Free. Claude does it.
Running tests? Free. Claude does it.

Implementation is free.
But the problem wasn't implementation.

Deciding what to build.
That's not free. AI can't do that. Only you can.

I skipped the decision and went straight to building.
"If I just start, something will come out."

Something came out.
Ten thousand lines of spaghetti.

"What if I just write better prompts?"
No. Prompts weren't the problem.

There was no destination.

What am I building?
What does it do?
Who uses it?
When is it done?

I had none of these four.
Didn't matter how good the prompts were.
The taxi just kept driving in circles.

items.title: [FDD Diary #5] Frustration Is the Spec
content:
Frustration becomes a spec.
A spec becomes a system.
A system becomes freedom.

They said I need to write a spec.

Spec? Like phone specs? RAM, storage, screen resolution?
That's the only "spec" I knew.

In software, spec means "a document that describes what you're building."

But I'm not a developer.
Never opened a document and typed "1. System Overview."
Never learned how.

Searched for how to write specs.
SRS. PRD. Functional specs.
All developer documents. Templates with fields and approval workflows.

"Non-functional requirements" — what?
"System constraints" — what?
"Use case diagram" — what?

I started vibe coding because I didn't want to learn coding.
Now you're telling me to learn spec writing?

So I just got pissed.

"Why doesn't KVM work?"
No network support.
Requirement: must connect over network.

"Why is Remote Desktop annoying?"
Slow. Drops connection.
Requirement: fast and stable.

"Why doesn't cloud work?"
Files only. No processes. And my files go through someone else's server.
Requirement: files AND commands. No cloud middleman.

Asked AI.
"Can I connect three computers directly? No cloud?"
"P2P is possible. But behind NAT, connections are tricky."
"What's NAT?"
"Behind a router. Most home networks."
"So how do you connect behind a router?"
"QUIC tunnels or STUN/TURN servers."
"What's that?"
Understood half of it.

Every "no" became a condition.
Twenty rounds of fighting.
Ask. Get told no. Hear why. Ask again.

I never opened a spec document.
Never typed "1. System Overview."
Never sat down to write a spec.

I got pissed.
Asked questions.
Fought.
Organized.

And the spec was already there.

"Nothing does this" is the current pain. That's the Reason.
"Work like one machine" is the change I want. That's the Purpose.
Same "why." Different answers.

"P2P connection" is the tech choice. That's the Method.
"Fork libp2p, check the MIT license" is how I get it. That's the Means.
Same "how." Different answers.

Purpose: Use multiple computers like one machine. From anywhere.
Reason: Nothing on the market does this. Everything is half-assed.
Method: Direct P2P connection. QUIC tunnels. Local-first.
Means: Open-source (quinn, libp2p), forked and adapted. MIT verified.

Four things.
That's a spec.
Not an SRS. Not a PRD.
Just organized frustration.

It doesn't come from a whiteboard in a conference room.
It comes from "why the hell doesn't this work."

Frustration is the Spec.

items.title: [FDD Diary #6] Everything Changed
content:
Once I had the spec, everything changed.

Day one.
AI tried to install a cloud SDK.
Showed it the spec. "It says no cloud. Right there."
AI came back. Switched to libp2p.

Before, I would've said "cool" and moved on.
Now I had the spec. Now I could say "that's wrong."

That's the difference.
Not better prompts. Not a smarter AI.
A piece of paper that says what I'm building.

For the first time, I wasn't following the AI.
The AI was following my spec.

And I could delete things.
For the first time, I could actually delete code.

Opened the ten-thousand-line codebase.
Found something not in the spec. Deleted it.
Found another. Deleted that too.

Three thousand lines left.
App didn't break. It got faster.

Forty-five minutes became twelve.
Python was pissing me off so I switched to Rust. It just got faster.
Failure rate dropped from 30% to 3%.

Seven thousand lines of code I couldn't read, couldn't understand, couldn't even tell if they belonged.
Gone.
And nothing broke.

Because now I knew what was supposed to be there.

I didn't know what a spec was.
I'm still not a "spec expert."

But I know one thing now.

Better prompts aren't the answer.
Better AI tools aren't the answer.
Knowing what you're building is the answer.

And that answer doesn't come out clean.
You get pissed. Ask questions. Fight. Organize.

Specs don't come from conference rooms.
They come from the grind.
